title: Your urge to breathe can lie to you
topic: What happens to your body when you hold your breath?

beats.label: breath hold
lines: Your urge to breathe can lie to you.

beats.title: During a breath hold
lines: When you hold your breath, oxygen reserves fall while carbon dioxide rises.
Your body keeps drawing on stored oxygen.
Here’s the twist: the urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising carbon dioxide, not falling oxygen.

beats.title: A breath-hold dive
lines: On a breath-hold dive, hyperventilating can delay that warning.
During ascent, falling pressure can drop oxygen sharply, causing blackout within seconds.

beats.text: Low oxygen is hard to sense
lines: Underwater, blackout can lead to drowning.
Low oxygen is hard to sense, so consciousness can fade without an obvious urge to breathe.
Prolonged oxygen deprivation can also injure neurons.
So the breath signal is more like a carbon-dioxide alarm than an oxygen gauge.
Don't hyperventilate before diving; stay within your limits and ascend slowly.

sources.claim: Breath-hold duration is limited by oxygen reserves and the response to rising carbon dioxide; the urge to breathe is driven mainly by rising carbon dioxide, and hyperventilation can delay warning signals.

During ascent, falling pressure can rapidly reduce available oxygen and cause blackout within seconds; blackout can lead to drowning, and safety guidance advises against pre-dive hyperventilation, staying within limits, and ascending slowly.
The body senses pure hypoxia poorly, so unconsciousness may occur without symptoms; prolonged hypoxia can cause neuronal cell death.
